newsitem.title: LEBANON: Red Army suspects were quiet neighbours.
newsitem.headline: Red Army suspects were quiet neighbours.

text.p: The neighbours thought Mariko Yamamoto was a company executive from the Philippines until last Saturday when armed men came at five a.m. to take her and fellow Red Army suspect Kazuo Tohira from her apartment.

Neighbours in west Beirut's crowded, lower middle class Corniche al-Mazraa district told Reuters that 56-year-old Yamamoto had lived quietly since last April on the eighth floor of a 10-storey apartment building.

"She was very quiet. We never imagined she could have possibly been a dangerous person until we saw them arrest her with her friend on Saturday," said Umm Mohammed, 37, a housewife living on the floor above Yamamoto.
"Whenever we met her she greeted us with a brief 'Marhaba' (Hello) and walked on," said another neighbour who identified herself as Wafa.
"If it wasn't for the smell of oriental spices coming out of her apartment at night we would have never noticed she was there," Wafa added.
Dressed usually in black trousers and a beige jacket, Yamamoto carried a black briefcase as she left home each morning. She returned after dark but none of the neighbours knew where she went.
"Every morning, between eight and nine a.m. she passed by to buy the English-language Daily Star newspaper," said Qassem al-Sayyed, 20, at a small stationery shop down the street.
Yamamoto's other stop was at Ghazi's grocery opposite the bookshop.
"She used to buy bread and cigarettes. She must have been a heavy smoker, buying more than one packet every day. I considered her one of my most polite clients," Ghazi, 50, said.
Umm Muhammed said the owner of the apartment building, a Lebanese resident of Saudi Arabia, told her when Yamamoto moved in last April that she was a Filipina with Spanish nationality.

"And that was all we ever knew about her. She often received guests, all with typical oriental looks. One used to spend nights with her," said Umm Muhammed, pointing to a newspaper photograph of Tohira, 44.

Umm Muhammed and other neighbours said a frequent visitor to Yamamoto's apartment was Masao Adachi, 57, another of the arrested Red Army suspects whom they identified from newspaper photographs. But they were not able to identify 49-year-old Kozo Okamoto.

Okamoto was involved in a May 1972 shootout at Tel Aviv's Lod airport in which 24 people died and 100 were wounded. He was captured by Israeli forces and sentenced to life imprisonment but was released in a Palestinian-Israeli prisoner swap in May 1985.
The plainclothes men ransacked Yamamoto's apartment after seizing her and Tohira, neighbours said.

"They took a lot of stuff out. Some boxes were open and I could see what looked like pieces of a photocopying machine. There were also a lot of plastic covers like those used to protect computers and printers," Umm Muhammed said.

Apart from Yamamoto and Tohira, security forces arrested three other Red Army suspects, three Japanese sympathisers and three Lebanese citizens in Lebanon's eastern Bekaa Valley at about the same time.

A lawyer for one of the Lebanese told Reuters at the Beirut palace of justice that two of the three Lebanese were quickly released but the third, acupuncture doctor Umayya Abboud, was still being held.

Authoritative sources in Tokyo told Reuters negotiations were under way between Japan and Lebanon to have the Japanese suspects, whom they described as five top members of the Red Army guerrilla group, deported, possibly by special plane.
